answer_text:
Let

\[
f_n(x)=nx^2\ln\left(1+\frac1{nx}\right),\qquad f(x)=x,\qquad x>0.
\]

For a fixed \(n>0\), make the substitution

\[
t=\frac{1}{nx}>0.
\]

Then \(x=\frac1{nt}\), and

\[
f_n(x)=n\left(\frac1{nt}\right)^2\ln(1+t)
=\frac{1}{n}\frac{\ln(1+t)}{t^2}.
\]

Also,

\[
f(x)=\frac1{nt}.
\]

Thus

\[
f_n(x)-f(x)
=\frac1n\left(\frac{\ln(1+t)}{t^2}-\frac1t\right)
=\frac1n\frac{\ln(1+t)-t}{t^2}.
\]

Since \(\ln(1+t)<t\) for \(t>0\), we have \(f_n(x)-f(x)<0\). Therefore

\[
|f_n(x)-f(x)|
=\frac1n\frac{t-\ln(1+t)}{t^2}.
\]

Now estimate

\[
t-\ln(1+t)
=\int_0^t \left(1-\frac1{1+s}\right)\,ds
=\int_0^t \frac{s}{1+s}\,ds.
\]

For \(s>0\),

\[
\frac{s}{1+s}<s,
\]

so

\[
0<t-\ln(1+t)<\int_0^t s\,ds=\frac{t^2}{2}.
\]

Hence

\[
0<\frac{t-\ln(1+t)}{t^2}<\frac12.
\]

So for every \(x>0\),

\[
|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\frac1{2n}.
\]

It remains to show this bound is sharp. As \(t\to0^+\), which corresponds to \(x\to\infty\),

\[
\lim_{t\to0^+}\frac{t-\ln(1+t)}{t^2}
=\frac12
\]

by L’Hôpital’s rule or the Taylor expansion \(\ln(1+t)=t-\frac{t^2}{2}+O(t^3)\). Therefore

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}|f_n(x)-f(x)|=\frac1{2n}.
\]

Thus the supremum exists but is not attained for finite \(x>0\). It is approached as \(x\to\infty\).

\[
\boxed{\frac{1}{2n}}
\]
